description: Glad to see you in my team!
summary: Outpost 30 is a free browser game for kids 7 to 12. You run a small Mars base for 30 sols (Mars days). Each sol you read a morning report and pick 2 of 3 cards, and every card costs something: air and water, power, or radiation shielding. There is no free "safe" choice. Real NASA space weather drives the danger: when online, the game pulls the last 30 days of solar flares and storms from NASA DONKI; offline it uses a saved copy and clearly says "archived, not live". Radiation uses the dose measured by the Curiosity RAD instrument, and radio delay to Earth uses JPL Horizons. Every number has a source button inside the game, and every science word gets a one-line explanation. Kip the guide can read text aloud for younger kids, teachers can share one class link so everyone plays the same mission, and the final debrief shows the 3 choices that mattered most, so kids want to play again. It needs no download, no account and works offline.
details:
What it does: Outpost 30 is a 10-minute mission game for kids 7 to 12. The player keeps a Mars base at Jezero crater alive for 30 sols (a sol is one Mars day, about 24 hours 40 minutes). There are only three bars: Life Support (air and water), Power, and Shield (how much radiation the crew can still safely take). Each sol the player reads a morning report and picks 2 of 3 cards. Every card has a visible cost and a benefit, so there is no free "safe" choice. Growing food is an action that costs power and water, not a fourth bar. Rank Cadet is for first missions (the crew always flies home safely); rank Commander is the full challenge.

How it uses real NASA data: Solar flares, CMEs and particle storms come from NASA DONKI. When the player is online the game loads the last 30 days live and shows a LIVE badge; offline it replays a saved real 30-day window and says "archived, not live". The daily radiation dose is the Curiosity RAD measurement (about 0.67 mSv per sol; the game says Jezero itself has no dosimeter). Radio delay on the Call Earth card uses JPL Horizons. Cards are tied to real missions and studies: MOXIE, ISS water recovery, Opportunity and InSight dust storms, NASA OSDR, and Canadian Space Agency food-in-space work. Every number has a source link and retrieval date inside the game, and numbers that are tuned for game balance are labelled as game numbers.

Why it teaches: Kids see that astronauts always trade one resource for another. A real flare gives about a day of warning, radiation adds up every day, and radio takes 11 to 20 minutes one way. Each science word gets a one-sentence explanation. After the mission a chart replays all 30 sols and names the 3 choices that mattered most, and kids can replay with a different 30 days of real data. Kip the guide can read text aloud, and teachers get one class link so everyone plays the same mission.

How we checked it: A simulator plays the real game engine 1,000 times per strategy. No single habit wins (Commander: smart planner 63%, random 3%, always shield 2%), so every choice has a cost. Browser tests cover phones from 320 px wide, keyboard play, reduced motion, and what happens when NASA's server is slow or down.

Tools: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript with no build step, no accounts and no tracking; the data is embedded so it works offline. Node.js scripts for testing and balancing, and Playwright for browser checks. Code, sources and the balance method are in the GitHub repository: https://github.com/shozy-frenia/junior-astronaut-trainer
dataRefs: NASA DONKI space weather database (flares, CMEs, particle storms)
NASA OSDR RadLab (ISS radiation dose measurements)
NASA JPL Horizons (Mars and Earth positions, sol length)
NASA Mars Fact Sheet (day length, gravity, atmosphere)
NASA MOXIE (oxygen made from Mars air)
NASA ISS water recovery system (Environmental Control and Life Support)
NASA OSDR study OSD-342 (space radiation biology data)
projectRefs: CSA: Growing healthy food in space and remote areas
CSA: Interplanetary farming activity (youth and educators)
